title: Modifiers, Parallelism and Grammatical Ambiguity
orientation: Accurate editing begins by finding the relationship a sentence expresses. A modifier can be grammatically positioned yet point to the wrong person; a neat-looking parallel list can still mix incompatible verb patterns; an apparently simple pronoun can leave two plausible referents. This lesson develops a method for diagnosing such problems without treating every unfamiliar construction as an error. You will first identify modifier targets and understood subjects, then examine attachment, scope, coordination and comparison. The final work checks whether a revision preserves time, participants, qualification and logical relations. Earlier knowledge of phrases, non-finite clauses, pronouns and coordination is useful. For open tasks, an explicit account of alternative readings is often more valuable than one silently guessed correction. The aim is to express an intended meaning clearly while retaining legitimate grammatical choices, including appropriate passive constructions and established variation.
outcomes: Identify a modifier’s target and a non-finite clause’s understood subject.
Explain at least two readings of an ambiguous attachment.
Distinguish not all from none and place only for an intended focus.
Construct coordination compatible with its shared head.
Verify that a proposed revision preserves meaning.

modules.title: Placing modifiers and recovering their subjects
modules.definition: A modifier adds descriptive or limiting information to another expression. A misplaced modifier suggests an unintended attachment; a dangling modifier lacks a suitable understood participant in its grammatical context.
foundation: Start by asking what each description is meant to describe. In a blue folder on the desk, blue describes the folder and on the desk locates it. In an opening participial clause such as Carrying a blue folder, Leena entered, Leena is normally understood as the person carrying the folder. Writing Carrying a blue folder, the door opened instead makes the door the expected carrier. The problem is not that the sentence begins with an -ing form; it is that the grammatical connection does not fit the intended event.
intermediate: Place a modifier close enough to its target that readers can recover the intended relationship. A notice reading We sell bags for children made of recycled fabric invites the absurd reading that children are made of fabric. We sell recycled-fabric bags for children removes that attachment risk. An introductory past-participial clause can correctly attach to a passive subject: Damaged in transit, the equipment was returned. Equipment is both what was damaged and what was returned; a passive main clause is not automatically a dangling construction.
advanced: A squinting modifier lies between expressions it could modify in either direction: Students who revise regularly improve. Regularly may describe revising or improvement. Rewrite around the intended message rather than move the word mechanically: Students who revise on a regular schedule improve, or Students who revise show regular improvement. Purpose infinitives need semantic care too. To reach the balcony, take the stairs has an understood imperative you; the absence of a printed subject does not make it faulty. To reach the balcony, the staircase is narrow gives no suitable controller of reach.
expert: The subject-sharing guideline governs ordinary subjectless adjunct clauses, not every initial expression. An absolute construction supplies its own subject: The inspection complete, the team left. Conventional comments such as generally speaking or to be honest concern the speaker’s stance and need not describe the next noun as an action. Some apparent dangling expressions are established discourse constructions; others create a real unintended assertion. Expert revision identifies the construction before applying a rule. If a person’s identity is unknown, use a finite clause or an impersonal alternative instead of inventing a named agent to repair the sentence.

patterns.form: Subjectless participial adjunct, + main subject + predicate
patterns.meaning: The understood participant normally matches the main subject.
An absolute can supply a different explicit subject.

examples.sentence: Walking beside the canal, Farah noticed the damaged railing.
examples.analysis: Farah is the walker and the observer.

examples.sentence: Stored below zero, the samples were stable for a week.
examples.analysis: The passive main subject also receives the storage action.

examples.sentence: The access road having flooded, the engineers postponed the visit.
examples.analysis: The absolute has its own subject, the access road.

contrasts.a: After examining the map, the route was obvious.
contrasts.b: After we examined the map, the route was obvious.
contrasts.note: The finite after-clause supplies the examiner; choose an actor only if the context identifies one.

exceptions: Conventional speaker comments such as Frankly speaking, the proposal is expensive do not require the proposal to speak.

mistakes.problem: Packed in ice, the courier delivered the fish.
mistakes.repair: The courier delivered the fish packed in ice.
mistakes.reason: The intended chilled entity is the fish, not the courier.

mistakes.problem: To pass the interview, punctuality is important.
mistakes.repair: To pass the interview, applicants should arrive punctually.
mistakes.reason: The revised infinitive has an understood actor; use this only where punctual arrival is actually the intended advice.

glossary.definition: An expression supplying an understood participant of a non-finite clause.
A supplementary construction with its own subject.
glossary.example: The rain having stopped, we left.

modules.title: Attachment, scope and reference
modules.definition: Ambiguity occurs when a form supports more than one interpretation. Attachment concerns which expression a modifier belongs to; scope concerns how much of a message an operator such as only or not affects.
foundation: A grammatical sentence can be ambiguous without containing an error. I photographed the guide with the telescope may mean that I used the telescope or that the guide had it. The prepositional phrase can attach to the photographing event or to the noun guide. To revise, state the intended interpretation: Using the telescope, I photographed the guide; or I photographed the guide who was carrying the telescope. Neither rewrite is the universally correct answer because the original supplies no decision between the two meanings.
intermediate: Scope differences are often created by focusing words. Only Salma reviewed the draft contrasts Salma with other possible reviewers. Salma reviewed only the draft contrasts that document with other possible objects. Salma only reviewed the draft can emphasise that she reviewed it rather than approved it, although spoken stress and context may support other readings. Keep the intended contrast explicit in formal prose. Negation interacts with quantifiers too: Not all the samples failed means at least some did not fail; none of the samples failed says that every sample avoided failure.
advanced: Pronoun reference requires a recoverable intended person or thing, but not every pronoun needs a single preceding noun. This can refer to an entire event: The lift stopped between floors. This delayed the delivery. That is a legitimate propositional reference. By contrast, When Hina met Sara, she was worried does not establish which woman was worried. Repeat a name or restructure the sentence if the distinction matters. Avoid solving ambiguity by guessing gender, role or a stereotype; preserve uncertainty when the source does not identify the intended referent.
expert: Grammatical ambiguity can coexist with pragmatic clarity. Context may make one reading overwhelmingly likely even though the structure permits another. Expert analysis separates a possible parse from a plausible intended meaning and identifies the evidence for each. Bound-variable readings also go beyond simple name replacement: Every researcher filed their own notes can vary the referent of their with each researcher. Do not replace such pronouns with one fixed name without changing meaning. Scope can remain underspecified intentionally, as in diplomatic language, but assessments must either supply enough context for one answer or explicitly reward the analysis of multiple readings.

patterns.meaning: Sets the constituent against contextually relevant alternatives.
Denies universality; it does not assert none.

examples.analysis: The focus excludes the other relevant servers from the set that failed.

examples.sentence: The manager did not approve every claim.
examples.analysis: This need not mean that the manager approved no claims.

examples.sentence: Each student labelled their own specimen.
examples.analysis: Their varies with each student; singular they need not identify one fixed person.

contrasts.a: The director spoke to the editor after her meeting.
contrasts.b: After the director’s meeting, the director spoke to the editor.
contrasts.note: The second explicitly selects one referent; it is appropriate only if that is the intended reading.

exceptions: Bare this is acceptable when its propositional referent is clear; adding a summary noun is a clarity tool, not a universal grammatical requirement.

mistakes.problem: Intended: some passed. None of the applicants failed the test.
mistakes.repair: Not all the applicants failed the test.
mistakes.reason: The original asserts universal success, which is stronger than the supplied meaning.

mistakes.problem: Intended meaning: I used my telescope to watch the visitor. Ambiguous wording: I watched the visitor with a telescope.
mistakes.repair: Using my telescope, I watched the visitor.
mistakes.reason: The revision fixes attachment without attributing a telescope to the visitor.

glossary.definition: The structural connection between a dependent and its head or clause.
glossary.example: the child with the red bag

glossary.definition: The domain over which a meaning operator applies.

modules.title: Parallelism, correlatives and comparisons
modules.definition: Parallelism presents related elements in comparable grammatical or conceptual forms. It supports clear comparison and coordination, while grammatical coordination ultimately depends on the functions and constructions involved.
foundation: Lists are easier to process when their parts follow a recognisable pattern: The role involves scheduling visits, checking records and answering enquiries. Each -ing clause fills the same complement position after involves. A mixture such as involves scheduling visits, record checks and to answer enquiries becomes awkward because the last infinitive does not fit the pattern. Try each element after the shared opening. If an item cannot combine with that opening, repair the structure rather than merely changing its ending to resemble the neighbouring words.
intermediate: Correlative pairs make structural expectations visible. The course is useful both for teachers and for editors places parallel prepositional phrases after both and and. The course both supports teachers and provides exercises coordinates verb phrases. Not only and but also can coordinate words, phrases or clauses. Fronted not only may require inversion in the clause it introduces, but it does not require every following item to be a full clause. Not only was the route shorter but also safer is a possible shared-copula construction; adding it was is another grammatical version.
advanced: Parallelism is not a rule that every coordinated unit must have an identical category label. A complement may coordinate expressions with a shared function: She is a capable editor and easy to work with can be understood as two predicative descriptions. Some mixed constructions are fully acceptable; others are confusing or disallowed by a particular head. In comparison, identify what is compared and what has been omitted. The new office is larger than the old one compares offices. The cost of the new office is higher than that of the old one compares costs, with that substituting for cost.
expert: Reduced comparison clauses rely on recoverable material: Mei reads more articles than I do clearly compares readers; Mei reads more articles than me may also have that informal standard reading. Mei likes Jo more than I can mean more than I like Jo, whereas Mei likes Jo more than me can mean more than she likes me. Avoid using a case preference to erase a genuine reading. Formal revisions can expand ellipsis to show the intended relationship. At expert level, examine syntactic compatibility, omitted material and logical comparability separately; rhythmic symmetry alone does not prove grammatical or semantic equivalence.

patterns.form: both X and Y / either X or Y
patterns.meaning: The paired constituents should fit the same construction and intended relationship.
Recover omitted material from context, or make it explicit.

examples.sentence: She plans to inspect the roof and to test the alarm.
examples.analysis: The two to-infinitives share a complementation role.

examples.sentence: Not only was the hall warmer but also quieter.
examples.analysis: The copula is shared with coordinated predicative adjectives.

examples.sentence: This week’s output exceeded last week’s output.
examples.analysis: The compared quantities are of the same relevant type.

contrasts.a: He enjoys reading and to cycle.
contrasts.note: Enjoy selects the relevant -ing complements; the repair addresses verb pattern as well as symmetry.

exceptions: Different forms can share a predicative function; evaluate the actual construction before declaring mixed categories ungrammatical.

mistakes.problem: She is interested in restoring clocks and to repair radios.
mistakes.repair: She is interested in restoring clocks and repairing radios.
mistakes.reason: The preposition in supports the coordinated -ing complements.

mistakes.problem: For a comparison of fares: The bus fare is lower than the train.
mistakes.repair: The bus fare is lower than the train fare.
mistakes.reason: The intended comparison is between fares, not a fare and a vehicle.

glossary.definition: Comparable form or organisation among related expressions.
glossary.example: to read, to draft and to edit

glossary.definition: One of a paired set signalling coordination.

modules.title: Predication and meaning-preserving revision
modules.definition: Predication attributes a property, identity or event to a subject. Faulty predication occurs when the expressed grammatical relationship fails to convey the intended logical relationship.
foundation: A sentence can be structurally well formed yet say something the writer did not intend. The aim of the workshop is improving attendance can be grammatical as an identification of an aim, whereas The cost of the workshop is because transport is expensive mixes a thing being measured with an unexplained causal clause. A clearer version is The workshop is expensive because transport costs are high. First decide what the subject refers to, then decide what the predicate says about it. Do not use logical oddness as an excuse to ban every uncommon subject–complement combination.
intermediate: Faulty comparison often arises when an abbreviated form conceals the wrong relationship. For the intended claim about income, Her salary is higher than her assistant invites comparison with a person rather than that person’s salary. Her salary is higher than her assistant’s makes the relation clear. Some compressed expressions are familiar idioms and need no repair: He earns more than his assistant can be a complete comparative clause with earns understood. The appropriate revision depends on what is syntactically omitted and what readers can reliably reconstruct.
advanced: Preserving meaning requires checking more than the topic. Did the original express every item or some items, possibility or certainty, a decision or a completed act, cause or sequence? The supervisor decided to close the office does not entail that the office closed. Because the equipment failed, the demonstration stopped asserts causation; The equipment failed and the demonstration stopped may leave the relation open. A grammatical revision that strengthens or changes these relationships is not a faithful correction, even when it sounds clearer. If the intended meaning is unavailable, offer alternatives and label their assumptions.
expert: Revision proceeds through diagnosis, interpretation, reconstruction and verification. Identify the smallest relevant structural unit, paraphrase its plausible readings, choose the intended one from evidence, then rebuild. Finally compare both versions for participants, time, polarity, quantification, modality, focus and register. Minimal editing is useful because it reduces unintended changes, but a small change is not automatically the best repair: it may preserve ambiguity or create a new presupposition. Expert editing sometimes needs a full finite clause rather than a compressed modifier. The objective is a defensible expression of the writer’s meaning, not obedience to a mechanical number-of-changes rule.

patterns.meaning: Attributes or identifies; check that the semantic relation is intended.
Verification includes scope, time, modality and participants.

examples.sentence: The reason for the delay was a missing permit.
examples.analysis: The complement identifies a cause rather than an unrelated location.

examples.sentence: The workshop was expensive because transport costs had risen.
examples.analysis: The because-clause gives the cause of expense.

examples.sentence: The board decided to suspend the scheme, but suspension had not yet begun.
examples.analysis: A decision is distinguished from its implementation.

contrasts.note: Both grammatical, but only the second asserts the action occurred.

exceptions: The reason ... is because occurs in established English; prefer an economical alternative where useful, but do not label every occurrence inherently ungrammatical.

mistakes.problem: Intended: costs are being compared. The repair cost is higher than a replacement device.
mistakes.repair: The repair cost is higher than the cost of a replacement device.
mistakes.reason: The supplied interpretation requires comparing two costs.

mistakes.problem: Original: Some inspections may be delayed. Proposed revision: All inspections will be delayed.
mistakes.reason: The proposed rewrite wrongly changes quantification and modal certainty.

glossary.definition: Attributing an event, property or identity to a subject.
A meaning that necessarily follows if a statement is true.
glossary.example: They left entails that departure occurred.

questions.prompt: Who is understood to be carrying the parcels in “Carrying two parcels, Asha rang the bell”?
questions.why: The ordinary subjectless participial adjunct shares its understood participant with main subject Asha.

questions.prompt: The intended carrier was the courier, not the parcel. Which rewrite expresses that?
options: The courier was entered by the carrying parcel.
Carrying a parcel, the courier entered.
Carrying a courier, the parcel entered.
The parcel, carrying a courier, entered.
questions.why: The main subject courier is a suitable understood carrier; the other versions reverse roles.

questions.prompt: Which statement means at least some claims were not approved, without saying none were approved?
options: Not all the claims were approved.
None of the claims was approved.
questions.why: Not all denies universal approval; none and no deny all approval, and every asserts it.

questions.prompt: Find the fault, if any: “Damaged in transit, the instruments were returned.”
questions.why: The instruments are both what were damaged and what were returned; passive main voice does not create a dangling modifier.

questions.prompt: Choose a complement pattern allowed by enjoy.
options: She enjoys drafting and to edit.
She enjoys to draft and editing.
questions.why: Enjoy selects the relevant -ing complements; the coordination must fit that head.

questions.prompt: For the explicit intended comparison of salaries, which sentence is clearest?
options: Her salary is higher her assistant.
Her assistant is higher salary than her.
Her salary is higher than her assistant.
Her salary is higher than her assistant’s salary.
questions.why: The second version explicitly compares salary with salary, preserving the stated intention.

questions.prompt: Which revision preserves “They decided to postpone the visit” without asserting the visit was postponed?
options: They reached a decision to postpone the visit.
questions.why: Reached a decision preserves the decision; implementation or cancellation is not entailed.

questions.prompt: In which example does This refer to the preceding event rather than identify or modify an object?
options: This is the notebook Nora lent me.
Please put this beside the other notebook.
The server failed. This interrupted the booking service.
questions.why: In the server example, This refers to the event of failure. In the other examples it modifies or identifies a concrete object in context.

questions.prompt: Identify the genuine error in “The position involves checking invoices, filing receipts and to answer calls.”
questions.why: The final to-infinitive does not fit the complements selected by involves here; answering calls fits.

questions.prompt: Which initial construction supplies its own explicit subject?
questions.why: The meeting finished is an absolute construction; meeting is its own explicit subject.

questions.prompt: Give two readings of I saw the inspector with binoculars.
questions.model: I used binoculars to see the inspector; or I saw the inspector who had binoculars.
rubric: Do not declare one reading mandatory.
alternatives: Other clear paraphrases of the two attachments are valid.

questions.prompt: Order for the intended focus “nobody except the librarian”: only / the librarian / could unlock / the cabinet.
questions.model: Only the librarian could unlock the cabinet.
rubric: Place only with the intended focus.
alternatives: The cabinet could be unlocked only by the librarian is also possible.

questions.prompt: Contrast Only Mina checked the forms / Mina checked only the forms.
questions.model: The first contrasts Mina with other checkers; the second contrasts forms with other objects.
alternatives: Context and spoken stress can refine the contrasts.

questions.prompt: Repair the intended description of a bag: We need a bag for the camera with a waterproof lining.
questions.model: We need a waterproof-lined bag for the camera.
rubric: Attach the lining to the bag.
Do not imply a waterproof camera.
alternatives: We need a bag with a waterproof lining for the camera is valid.

questions.prompt: Identify the subject of the participial clause in The rain having stopped, the players returned.
questions.model: The rain is the explicit subject of having stopped; the players is the main-clause subject.
alternatives: Absolute participial clause is acceptable terminology.

questions.prompt: Combine as parallel -ing complements: The job involves booking rooms. It involves checking tickets. It involves answering queries.
questions.model: The job involves booking rooms, checking tickets and answering queries.
alternatives: Repeating involves or using a finite coordination can also be grammatical.

questions.prompt: Split without losing causation: Because the lift failed, the delivery team used the stairs.
questions.model: The lift failed. As a result, the delivery team used the stairs.
alternatives: The lift failed, so ... is a valid one-sentence alternative but does not satisfy the requested split.

questions.prompt: Why is We planned to reopen not equivalent to We reopened?
questions.model: A plan can remain unimplemented; reopened asserts that reopening occurred.
alternatives: An original counterexample is valid.

questions.prompt: Classify generally speaking in Generally speaking, the route is safe as a literal action by route or a speaker comment.
questions.model: It is a conventional speaker comment introducing a generalisation.
rubric: Do not call it dangling solely because route cannot speak.
alternatives: Comment adjunct is acceptable terminology.

questions.prompt: Complete a parallel list with forms of prepare, check and send: Her duties include ____ orders, ____ addresses and ____ confirmations.
questions.model: preparing orders, checking addresses and sending confirmations
alternatives: Coherent complete noun phrases may work, but must satisfy the supplied verb-form task.

questions.prompt: A note says When Naila met Uzma, she was worried. Give two explicit revisions without choosing which is factually true.
questions.model: When Naila met Uzma, Naila was worried. / When Naila met Uzma, Uzma was worried.
rubric: Resolve reference differently in each version.
Do not add a cause for the worry.
alternatives: Equivalent restructuring is valid.

questions.prompt: Use both ... and to coordinate two objects: The course supports teachers. It also supports editors.
questions.model: The course supports both teachers and editors.
alternatives: The course both supports teachers and supports editors is grammatical but coordinates verb phrases instead.

questions.prompt: Correct for the intended fare comparison: The taxi fare is higher than the bus.
questions.model: The taxi fare is higher than the bus fare.
rubric: Keep higher rather than change the claim.
alternatives: ... higher than that of the bus is possible.

questions.prompt: Explain why a comma alone cannot establish who used a telescope in I photographed the guide with a telescope.
questions.model: The ambiguity concerns the prepositional phrase’s attachment. Explicitly naming the user or expanding a relative clause is safer than relying on a comma.
alternatives: A carefully contextualised punctuation solution may work; explain the context.

questions.prompt: Edit for the stated intentions: the courier carried ice, the samples were cold, and a decision had not been implemented. “Carrying a box of ice, the samples arrived cold. We decided to postpone the test, so the test was postponed.”
questions.model: The courier arrived carrying a box of ice, and the samples were cold. We decided to postpone the test, but the postponement had not yet been implemented.
rubric: Supply courier as carrier from the context.
Do not equate decision with implementation.
alternatives: Other faithful versions are valid.

questions.prompt: Can non-identical grammatical categories ever be coordinated? Use She is a lawyer and proud of her work.
questions.model: Yes. A noun phrase and an adjective phrase can both serve predicatively here; identical labels are not an absolute requirement.
alternatives: Framework-specific category labels are acceptable if the shared function is clear.

questions.prompt: Complete the intended two-cost comparison: The cost of repair exceeded ____ of replacement.
rubric: Use substitution for the singular cost.
alternatives: The cost can be repeated in an expanded sentence.

questions.prompt: Write two sentences using not all and none; explain why they make different claims.
questions.model: Not all the lamps worked: two remained dark. None of the spare lamps worked: every spare was faulty.
rubric: Supply contexts matching each quantifier scope.
Do not equate partial failure with universal failure.
alternatives: Any natural examples preserving the scope distinction are valid.

corrections.prompt: Repair; the chef, not the soup, tasted it: Tasting the soup, the seasoning seemed weak.
corrections.model: When the chef tasted the soup, the seasoning seemed weak.
rubric: Keep the evaluation uncertain with seemed.
alternatives: The chef found the seasoning weak when tasting the soup is possible.

corrections.prompt: Repair the list selected by avoid: We avoid delaying payments and to lose receipts.
corrections.model: We avoid delaying payments and losing receipts.
alternatives: A finite rewrite is acceptable if meaning is preserved.

corrections.prompt: Clarify; the editor had the red notebook: I interviewed the editor with a red notebook.
corrections.model: I interviewed the editor who had a red notebook.
rubric: Do not make the notebook an interview instrument.
alternatives: I interviewed the red-notebook-carrying editor is possible but heavier.

corrections.prompt: Decide whether correction is required: Stored in sealed jars, the spices were protected from moisture.
alternatives: An active rewrite is optional, not an obligatory correction.

corrections.prompt: Repair for a comparison of processing times: Our processing time is shorter than the rival service.
corrections.model: Our processing time is shorter than the rival service’s processing time.
alternatives: ... shorter than that of the rival service is valid.

corrections.prompt: Clarify the intended exclusion of other reviewers: Farah only reviewed the draft.
alternatives: Farah was the only person who reviewed the draft is valid.

corrections.prompt: Correct only if necessary: The staff were arguing among themselves about the rota.
corrections.model: No change is required in British English.
alternatives: The staff members were ... is an explicit alternative.

corrections.prompt: Repair without inventing an outcome: Some grants may be delayed → proposed “All grants will be delayed”.
corrections.model: Keep Some grants may be delayed.
alternatives: An equivalent paraphrase must preserve both limitations.

transformations.prompt: Combine using a subjectless participial clause. The technician checked the seal. The technician opened the container. Keep the sequence explicit.
transformations.model: Having checked the seal, the technician opened the container.
alternatives: After checking the seal, the technician opened the container is valid.

transformations.prompt: Rewrite to remove ambiguity; meaning intended: Sara likes Amina more than Sara likes the speaker. Original: Sara likes Amina more than me.
transformations.model: Sara likes Amina more than Sara likes me.
rubric: Keep Sara as liker in both clauses.
alternatives: Sara likes me less than she likes Amina is equivalent.

writing.prompt: Write a 100–140-word project update containing one participial opening, one correlative coordination and one limited claim. Then name a possible ambiguity you deliberately avoided. Invent the scenario and do not present invented statistics as real evidence.
writing.model:
Having inspected the storeroom, the team recommended both replacing the damaged shelf and labelling the sealed boxes. Some deliveries may be delayed while the room is reorganised, but the team has proposed an alternative collection point near reception. Amina discussed that proposal with Leena after the inspection. Amina supported the temporary move, while Leena asked for clearer signs before it began. The manager has not yet approved the proposal, so staff should continue using the existing instructions until a revised notice is issued. This update identifies a possible disruption without presenting a recommendation as a completed change or claiming that every delivery will be affected.

Analysis: The opening participle belongs to the team. Both…and coordinates two -ing clauses. Some…may is limited. Repeating Amina distinguishes her view from Leena’s instead of leaving she ambiguous.
rubric: Identify the controller of the opening participle.
Make both correlative items fit the shared construction.
Preserve a limited quantifier and a modal qualification.
Explain an actual ambiguity risk and its revision.
alternatives: Any original coherent update meeting the conditions is valid; this is self-review, not an automatic writing grade.

recall.prompt: Recall Day 21: Does The director advised me to complain prove that I complained?
recall.model: No; advice need not be followed.
rubric: Do not infer an unstated event.
alternatives: An original counterexample is acceptable.

recall.prompt: Recall Day 13: Identify the head in the large bag on the shelf.
recall.model: Bag is the head of the noun phrase; on the shelf postmodifies it.
alternatives: Terminological variants are acceptable.

recall.prompt: Recall Day 17: Compare The sample may be contaminated / The sample must be contaminated in a deduction context.
recall.model: May expresses possibility; must expresses a strong deduction from evidence.
rubric: Do not read must as a command here.
alternatives: Equivalent degrees-of-confidence explanations are valid.

checklist: I diagnose the relationship rather than label an unusual word wrong.
I can distinguish an absolute from an ordinary subjectless adjunct.
I check the meaning of quantifiers and modal verbs after editing.
I can expand a comparison to reveal its intended participants.
